title: Μύρμηξ καὶ κάνθαρος
part: The Ant and the Beetle (Chambry 241 · Perry 112)
source: Émile Chambry, Ésope: Fables, texte établi et traduit (Les Belles Lettres, Paris, 1927), fable 241 (= Perry 112). Text as printed, including Chambry's editorial punctuation (« »). Pronunciation: reconstructed Attic, after W. S. Allen, Vox Graeca. Romanization: standard classical transliteration (ē/ō; th/ph/ch; y for υ, u in diphthongs; h = rough breathing; ēi/āi/ōi for iota subscript; accents omitted).

sentences.t: Θέρους ὥρᾳ μύρμηξ περιπατῶν κατὰ τὴν ἄρουραν πυροὺς καὶ κριθὰς συνέλεγεν, ἀποθησαυριζόμενος ἑαυτῷ τροφὴν εἰς τὸν χειμῶνα.
sentences.tr: Therous hōrāi myrmēx peripatōn kata tēn arouran pyrous kai krithas synelegen, apothēsaurizomenos heautōi trophēn eis ton cheimōna.
sentences.l: In summer's season an ant, walking about over the ploughland, was gathering wheat and barley, storing up food for himself against the winter.
sentences.n: Θέρους ὥρᾳ is a dative of time with the genitive of the season, 'at the season of summer' — the same opening as the ants' fable at 336, which begins Χειμῶνος ὥρᾳ. εἰς with the accusative looks forward in time: laid up for the winter, against its coming.

sentences.t: Κάνθαρος δὲ τοῦτον θεασάμενος ἐθαύμασεν ὡς ἐπιπονώτατον, εἴγε παρ’ αὐτὸν τὸν καιρὸν μοχθεῖ παρ’ ὃν τὰ ἄλλα ζῷα πόνων ἀφειμένα ῥᾳστώνην ἄγει.
sentences.tr: Kantharos de touton theasamenos ethaumasen hōs epiponōtaton, eige par’ auton ton kairon mochthei par’ hon ta alla zōia ponōn apheimena rhāistōnēn agei.
sentences.l: But a beetle, having beheld him, marvelled at him as most laborious, seeing that he toils at that very season at which the other animals, released from labours, keep their ease.
sentences.i: A beetle who saw him marvelled at how hard he worked, since he was labouring at the very season when every other creature is let off its labours and takes its ease.
sentences.n: The κάνθαρος is the dung-beetle, which lives off the droppings the warm months leave lying about and so has nothing whatever to do in summer — the whole fable turns on that. ὡς with the superlative ἐπιπονώτατον gives the ground of the wonder as the beetle sees it, not as a fact vouched for. εἴγε, 'seeing that', introduces the reason he assumes. ἀφίημι takes the genitive of what one is released from (πόνων); ῥᾳστώνην ἄγειν is 'to keep holiday, live at ease'.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ τότε μὲν ἡσύχαζεν· ὕστερον δέ, ὅτε χειμὼν ἐνέστη, τῆς κόπρου ὑπὸ τοῦ ὄμβρου ἐκλυθείσης, ὁ κάνθαρος ἧκε πρὸς αὐτὸν λιμώττων καὶ τροφῆς μεταλαβεῖν δεόμενος.
sentences.tr: Ho de tote men hēsychazen· hysteron de, hote cheimōn enestē, tēs koprou hypo tou ombrou eklytheisēs, ho kantharos hēke pros auton limōttōn kai trophēs metalabein deomenos.
sentences.l: But he for the moment kept quiet; and later, when winter had set in, the dung having been dissolved by the rain, the beetle came to him famishing and begging to have a share of food.
sentences.i: The ant held his peace at the time; but later, when winter had set in and the rain had dissolved the dung away, the beetle came to him starving and begged for a share of his food.
sentences.n: τότε μέν looks ahead to ὕστερον δέ, the pair holding the two halves of the story apart — a shape worth watching for, since Greek regularly announces a contrast before it arrives. A genitive absolute (τῆς κόπρου … ἐκλυθείσης) supplies the reason the beetle is destitute: ἐκλύω is to loosen and break up, so the winter rain simply dissolves his larder. μεταλαμβάνω, 'get a share of', takes the genitive, and δεόμενος governs the infinitive.

sentences.t: Ὁ δὲ ἔφη πρὸς αὐτόν· « Ὦ κάνθαρε, ἀλλ’ εἰ τότε ἐπόνεις, ὅτε ἐμόχθουν καὶ ἐμὲ ὠνείδιζες, οὐκ ἂν νῦν τροφῆς ἐπεδέου. »
sentences.tr: Ho de ephē pros auton· « Ō kanthare, all’ ei tote eponeis, hote emochthoun kai eme ōneidizes, ouk an nyn trophēs epedeou. »
sentences.l: But he said to him: « O beetle, if you had been working then, when I was toiling and you were reproaching me, you would not now be in want of food. »
sentences.n: An unreal condition: imperfect in the protasis, imperfect with ἄν in the apodosis, and τότε and νῦν dividing the time between the halves — 'if you had been at work then, you would not be in want now'. ἐπιδέομαι, 'be in need of', takes the genitive. ὀνειδίζω more usually takes the dative of the person reproached; the accusative ἐμέ here is the later usage, and is what Chambry prints.

sentences.t: Οὕτως οἱ παρὰ τὰς εὐθηνείας τοῦ μέλλοντος μὴ προνοούμενοι παρὰ τὰς τῶν καιρῶν μεταβολὰς τὰ μέγιστα δυστυχοῦσιν.
sentences.tr: Houtōs hoi para tas euthēneias tou mellontos mē pronooumenoi para tas tōn kairōn metabolas ta megista dystychousin.
sentences.l: So those who through the times of plenty take no forethought for what is coming fare most wretchedly at the turns of the seasons.
sentences.n: παρά with the accusative twice over, both times of time: 'all through the seasons of plenty' and 'at the turns of the year'. προνοέομαι takes the genitive of what is provided for (τοῦ μέλλοντος, 'the thing that is to come'); μή rather than οὐ because the participle describes a class of men, not a particular fact. τὰ μέγιστα is an adverbial accusative, 'to the greatest degree'.
